answer_1:
White is decisively better (+454cp), and the engine's first choice is 46. Qe7+, a check that keeps the initiative.

**What's forcing.** Black's queen on f5 attacks the pawns on e5 and g5, so White wants to keep the initiative with checks. Qe7+ attacks the king on g7 and the pawns on e6 and a7 while still defending g5. In the engine's line, Black replies Qf7, then 47. Qf6+ Kg8 48. Nc4 Qe8 49. Na5 Qc8. The queen on f6 attacks e6 and g6, and the knight on c4 defends e3 and e5 before heading to a5, where it attacks the c6 pawn. No material changes hands in that line, so the gain is positional.

**The long-term picture.** White's structure is slightly better, mainly because Black has isolated pawns on a7, c6 and e6. Black's king is also far more exposed than White's, which is the biggest factor in the position. White has the extra knight.

**Alternatives.** Qc7+ and Qd7+ are slightly worse. The engine sees something the positional factors don't show. Both lines win a pawn, but the engine still puts Qe7+ first.

**What to aim for.** Keep checking, keep the e5 and g5 pawns defended, and bring the knight toward a5 to hit c6. Use the exposed black king to keep Black's queen tied down.

Black is decisively better here (about -254cp), mostly because White is down 6 points of material: Black has an extra rook and pawn. The engine's first choice is Bxc6, the idea being to remove Black's active knight, the only piece attacking the e5 pawn besides the queen, and to keep the position as stable as possible.

Nothing is forcing right now. The Black queen on c7 pins the e5 pawn to the bishop on f4, and the a6 pawn attacks White's bishop on b5, so the bishop must decide what to do. Bxc6 resolves that: the line runs 13. Bxc6 Qxc6 14. Rc1 Qb5 15. Nc4 Bb7 16. a4 Qb4. Material stays the same, since the trade is a bishop for a knight. White gets the rook onto the open c-file with tempo against the queen, and the knight on c4 helps defend e5.

Long-term, White does have some compensation in the factors: its pieces are more mobile, its king is safer, and Black's queen is more exposed to pins. Black counters with a slightly better pawn structure and bishops that work better. Those pluses are small next to the material deficit.

Ba4 is only slightly worse by the engine's count, and the engine sees something the listed factors do not show. Bd3 is a bit further behind.

To play on, aim to use the open b- and c-files, keep e5 defended, and look for activity before Black finishes developing the bishops on c8 and f8 and the knight on g8.

Black has a clear advantage, and White's best practical try is 20. Qxf6, grabbing the bishop that has just landed on f6. White is a piece down at the moment, so this is a recovery job.

**What's forcing:** Black's queen on a5 pins the rook on d2 to the king on e1, so that rook can't move. Black also has the knight check on d3 in hand. In the engine's line, 20. Qxf6 Nd3+ 21. Kd1 Qxe5 22. Qxe5 Nxe5 23. Nd4 Nd7, the queens come off and White wins back 2 points, leaving Black only 1 point ahead. It is the engine's top choice because it leaves Black the smallest edge of the three moves it lists.

20. exf6 looks natural, since the pawn takes the bishop, but after 20... Nd3+ 21. Kd1 Qxa2 Black's queen picks up the a2 pawn, and the line ends with Black 3 points ahead. 20. Nc3 allows 20... Bxe5 and runs into Nd3+ again, leaving Black 4 points ahead.

**Long-term picture:** White's king is the main problem, as king safety favours Black heavily. It's stuck on e1 with the d2 rook pinned and the queen on h6 far from home. Black also has more mobile pieces. White does have small edges in rook placement and bishops, but they don't offset the exposed king.

A club player would lean toward White here, but the pin and the d3 check make White's position harder than it looks.

**Going forward:** Aim to trade queens to relieve the king, then use the d-file and the knight on d4 to pressure e6 while Black's extra material is reduced.

The position is equal (about a quarter of a pawn for White, within the normal opening range). The engine's first choice is 7. dxc5, with 7. c4 only 6cp behind, so don't call either better. The idea is to resolve the tension in the centre: your d4 pawn is attacked by both Black's c5 pawn and the knight on c6, and dxc5 takes the c5 pawn rather than waiting to be captured.

White is decisively better. The engine's first choice is 22. gxh5, hitting the queen on g6 with the pawn and opening Black's king.

**What's forcing:** The pawn on g4 attacks h5, and Black's queen on g6 is overloaded. It defends the pawn on h5, the pawn on c6 and the bishop on f7. In the engine's line, Black replies 22... Qxh5 23. Ng3 Qh8, and then White's queen gets a run of checks: Qe7+, Qd8+, Nf5+, Qh4+ and Qg5+. That ends with the queen on g5 pinning the bishop on g7 to the king on g8. No material is won, but Black's king is stripped of cover and the queen is pushed back to h8.

Nothing is forcing. Black's Knight on f6 attacks the pawn on e4, but that pawn is defended by the Bishop on c2, so there is no immediate threat to deal with. That leaves room for a useful quiet move.

The long-term picture is balanced. Pawn structure, king safety and space are level, with no weaknesses on either side. Black has a slight mobility edge, since White's pieces have fewer safe squares. White's Bishop on c1 and Knight on b1 are still at home, so improving them is the practical task.

Aim to bring the queenside pieces into play, perhaps with Na3 or Re1, and to cover e4 so Black's knight has nothing to bite on. Then your mobility catches up with Black's.

The idea behind g3 is to support the f4 pawn and the knight on h4, which Black's bishop on e7 is attacking. Nothing is forcing at the moment apart from that attack on the knight, so White's task is to settle it safely.

The engine's line runs 13. g3 Ba6 14. Ng2 g5 15. O-O-O gxf4 16. Nxf4 g5. White's knight reroutes to g2 and then f4, and the king castles long. At the moment the d4 and f4 pawns both hold up the e5 pawn.

Aim to keep the knight safe, finish development by castling, and use the f-file as the g-pawns get exchanged. Avoid grabbing the g6 pawn.

The long-term picture is close to balanced. Pawn structure, knights, bishops, rooks, space and the queens all come out about even. The one gap is king safety, where Black is a little ahead. White's king is still on e1 with its bishop on f1 undeveloped, so castling is the natural way to fix that.

Aim to get the bishop to g2, castle, and then fight for the centre with d4 or Nc3.

The position is roughly equal, at about 10 centipawns. The engine's first choice is 6. exd4, simply recapturing the pawn Black just took on d4. That restores material and leaves Black's d-file pawns (d5, d4) no longer doubled, while White's pawn on d4 keeps a firm central grip.

Nothing is forcing right now. Black's pawn on d4 attacks White's pawn on e3, but recapturing settles that at once. The other options teach something too. 6. Bb5+ and 6. Nxd4 are both about 40 centipawns worse, though still roughly equal. Bb5+ trades off bishops, and the engine's line ends with king safety moving well towards Black. Nxd4 invites ...Bf6 and later ...Bxb2, leaving White with isolated a- and c-pawns.

Long term, White has a bit more mobility, but Black's king is safer by the engine's king-safety measure. Black also has slightly more space.

The engine's line, 6. exd4 Qb6 7. Nbd2 Qxb2 8. Rb1 Qc3 9. Rb3 Qa5, shows the main danger: Black's queen raids the b2 pawn. The engine still judges the line roughly equal, because it sees the material won back or enough in return beyond these moves. Even so, a club player might feel White is more comfortable here.

Aim to recapture on d4, then develop the b1 knight and bishop, and get the king safe. Watch for queen raids along the b-file and the pin on d2 against the king.

White has a slight advantage, and the engine's first choice is 19. Qd2. Nothing is forcing here: no checks or tactics decide the position, so this is a battle of placement.

The long-term picture favours White mainly through king safety. Black's king on e8 is the more exposed one. The other factors (pawn structure, space, mobility, rooks) are about even, so White's edge is modest and rests mainly on king safety.

Qd2 is a regrouping move. In the engine's line, 19. Qd2 Bd7 20. Nd1 f6 21. c3 Nc6 22. Ne3 a5, White uses c3 to kick the knight off d4 and puts its own knight on e3, where it defends the bishop on d5 and the pawn on f5. Nb1 is also about as good, so do not call either better.

A club player would clearly prefer White here.

To play this well, keep the pieces protecting the bishop on d5 and the pawns on e4 and f5, and drive the black knight away from d4 with c3. Rf2 is a good alternative if you want to support the f5 pawn first.

answer_1:
Black has a slight advantage here, and White's best move, Qxf7+, is the least bad of a difficult set. **What's forcing.** White's queen on c4 pins Black's queen on f7 to the king on g8, so the queen has only three moves: Qe6, Qd5 or Qxc4. White can cash in on that with Qxf7+ Bxf7, then Rxa6 bxa6 bxc6. This wins a knight and a pawn but gives up a rook, which cancels White's one-point lead and leaves material level. The engine continues with Ba5, hitting the knight on c3, and Rc1 Rc8, with Black's rook attacking the pawn on c6. White gets passed pawns on c6 and d4 out of it.

**The alternatives fail.** Ra4 allows cxb5, and the line ends with Black a point ahead and a clear advantage. Qa4 is worse still, since Bxa5 wins the rook on a5 and leaves Black with a decisive advantage.

**The long-term picture.** White has more mobile pieces, and the bishop on e5 is active. But White's d4 pawn is isolated, and Black has the better pawn structure. White also has a loose rook on a5 that the bishop on d8 attacks, and that is why the tactics matter so much.

**What to aim for.** Trade queens with Qxf7+, then use the passed pawns on c6 and d4 as your main assets. Keep the knight on c3 defended, since Black's bishop on a5 will target it.

answer_1:
White has a slight advantage here. The engine's first choice is 5. cxd5, with 5. Qa4+ and 5. g3 close behind, so the choice among them is mostly one of style.

Nothing is forcing. No pieces are hanging and nothing is pinned. The tension is in the centre: White's pawn on c4 and knight on c3 both attack Black's pawn on d5, and Black's d5 pawn attacks c4.

The idea behind 5. cxd5 is to resolve that tension on White's terms. The engine line runs 5. cxd5 exd5 6. Bf4 Nf6 7. e3 O-O 8. Bd3 c5. White wins no material. The gain is positional: after the exchange White's pieces get more room, the bishops improve, and the pawn structure improves a little. Bf4 develops the c1 bishop outside the pawn chain, and Bd3 then aims at h7.

The long-term picture explains why White is better. White's king is safer, while space is roughly level. Black's pawn structure currently scores slightly better, which is why improving it is one of the line's aims. Mobility and bishop placement are roughly level, but White still has both bishops at home and Black has three pieces undeveloped (Bc8, Nb8, Ng8), so White can use the tempo to build a comfortable position.

Qa4+ is about as good, and so is the quieter g3. None of the three is better than the others.

From here, aim to develop the c1 bishop actively, support the d4 pawn with e3, and bring the f1 bishop out to a useful diagonal.

Black has a clear advantage here, mainly because of the six-point material edge: Black has an extra rook and an extra pawn, since White has only five pawns to Black's six. The engine's first choice is Ned6+, with Be3 and Qd1 about as good, so none of the three is better than the others.

The forcing move is the check Ned6+. Black's Knight on b4 also attacks the Pawn on a2 and the Bishop on d3. The Knight check on d6 hits the King on e8, the Pawn on f7 and the Bishop on c8. That line shifts king safety toward Black, so it isn't a clean improvement, but it keeps pieces active and gives White's bishops more scope.

The engine does not give a reason beyond these factors for preferring Ned6+ over Be3 or Qd1, since it rates them about equal.

A club player would clearly prefer Black, matching the material count.

White has a slight advantage here, and the engine's first choice is 5. Bf4. It develops the c1-bishop with tempo, since it attacks the Black queen on c7, and it also keeps the g3 pawn defended after the queen's pressure on it.

Nothing else is forcing. White has no immediate tactics, and the only pressure on the board is the queen on c7 eyeing g3 and the tension between the c4 and d5 pawns.

The engine line runs 5. Bf4 Qd8 6. cxd5 cxd5 7. Bg2 g6 8. O-O Bg7. In it Black's queen steps back, which costs a tempo, and White then castles with the bishop on g2 and the knight on f3 well placed. The line gains nothing in material. It improves White's king safety, which is the main thing it changes.

Right now Black's king safety is ahead, but White has a small mobility edge, and pawn structure, space, knights, bishops and rooks are about even. So the plan is to develop smoothly and use the tempo on the queen.

5. d4 and 5. Bg2 are about as good as Bf4, so you can't call any of the three clearly better. d4 stakes out the centre, while Bg2 gets ready to castle.

From here, aim to finish development with Bf4, Bg2 and castling, and keep the c-file in mind, since it opens after cxd5 cxd5. A club player would clearly prefer White's position.

**What's forcing:** Nothing urgent. Your bishop on b5 pins the knight on c6 to the king on e8, so that knight can't move, but no tactic is on the board yet. The pin is a useful pressure point rather than a threat.

**The idea behind d4:** It challenges Black's pawn on c5 and opens the centre while Black's king is still on e8 and Black's bishops and knight on g8 are undeveloped. In the engine line, 6. d4 cxd4 7. Nxd4 Bd7 8. O-O Nf6 9. Nc3 Bd6, you recapture with the knight on d4, which hits the c6 knight. Black ends up with an isolated pawn on d5 and an open c-file. The line favours White in knight placement and rooks, while Black gets somewhat better king safety. The engine calls Nc3 and O-O about as good, so do not rank them against d4.

**Long-term picture:** The factors are close. Black has a slight mobility edge: it has a little more safe room for its pieces, while White's bishop on c1 and knight on b1 are still at home. Only two White pieces, Bb5 and Nf3, are developed, so getting the rest out matters. Castling would also finish your king's safety.

**What to aim for:** Develop quickly, castle, and use d4 to leave Black with the isolated d5 pawn to target, as the engine's lines do.

**What's forcing.** Black's last move, 31...Qxd5, left the queen en prise to the e4 pawn. In the engine's line, 32. exd5 Re8 33. Qxa6 Nf6 34. Rc8 Bxd5 35. Rxe8+ Nxe8, White ends up nine points ahead. The queen is won, and in the engine's line Black's counterplay only wins back a pawn with Bxd5 and a rook with Nxe8, after White's own rook has taken Black's rook on e8. Note that Black's bishop on g5 pins the knight on d2 to the rook on c1, so White should watch that pin, but it doesn't stop the capture.
